alignment.note: The adverb εὐθὺς ('immediately') is rendered by the Vulgate's statim and is fused into the Syriac ܘܡܚܕܐ, which prefixes the conjunction ('and at once') into a single word; thus the Greek conjunction-plus-adverb sequence is collapsed into one lexeme in Syriac.

Greek and Latin express 'his disciples' analytically (article + noun + possessive pronoun; discipulos suos), whereas Syriac ܠܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ synthesises the object marker, noun, and 3ms possessive suffix into a single inflected word.

Greek ἐμβῆναι εἰς τὸ πλοῖον ('to embark into the boat') and the Syriac ܕܢܣܩܘܢ ('that they should go up/board') use a complementary subordinate verb of motion, while the Vulgate ascendere navim drops the preposition and takes the boat as a direct object; the Syriac additionally shifts from infinitive to a finite imperfect with a subjunctival prefix.

Greek καὶ προάγειν ('and to go before') is a coordinated infinitive; the Vulgate recasts it as a purpose clause ut præcederent eum ('that they might precede him'), supplying the object eum; Syriac ܘܢܐܙܠܘܢ ܩܕܡܘܗܝ ('and that they should go before him') likewise adds the explicit pronominal object 'him' absent in the Greek.

The Greek prepositional phrase εἰς τὸ πέραν ('to the other side') with articular substantive is matched by the Vulgate trans fretum ('across the strait'), which specifies the body of water, while the Syriac ܠܥܒܪܐ uses a single substantive from the root ʿ-b-r ('crossing/far side').
ἕως αὐτὸς / ܥܕ ... ܗܘ / dum ipse

The Greek present indicative ἀπολύει ('he dismisses') stands in a temporal clause where both the Vulgate dimitteret (imperfect subjunctive) and the Syriac ܫܪܐ (perfect/general) adjust the verbal aspect to fit their respective temporal-clause syntax; the difference is purely grammatical.
